## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Tevijjavaccha Sutta* (MN 71) is a discourse in the Majjhimanikāya addressed to the wanderer Vacchagotta [SuttaCentral; Le 2018]. In the dialogue, Vacchagotta asks whether rumours that the Buddha is omniscient (*sabbaññū*) and all-seeing—having uninterrupted vision continuously present while walking, standing, sleeping, or awake—are accurate [Saitanaporn 2009; The Yakherds 2019; Le 2018]. The Buddha rejects this claim, explaining that asserting he knows and sees all things simultaneously misrepresents him [The Yakherds 2019; Le 2018]. Instead, he describes his attainment in terms of the threefold higher knowledge (*tevijjā*): recollection of past lives, knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their karma, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints or defilements (*āsava*) [Pande 1974; Le 2018; SuttaCentral]. When asked about other sects, the Buddha also observes that in the past ninety-one aeons he knows of only one Ājīvika who reached heaven, doing so because that individual believed in the efficacy of karma [Appleton, Narrating Karma and Rebirth].

SuttaCentral identifies the *Cūḷadukkhakkhandha Sutta* (MN 14) as a full and partial parallel, and notes that the sutta is referenced in the Kathāvatthu (Kv 4.1, *Gihissaarahātikathā*) [SuttaCentral]. In DharmaNexus match data, the text shares 853 text-reuse segments across 83 Pali texts, showing extensive internal parallels with the *Nidāna Saṁyutta* (SN 12), *Gāmaṇi Saṁyutta* (SN 42), *Sandaka Sutta* (MN 76), *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Cūḷasakuludāyi Sutta* (MN 79), and the *Kaṇṇakatthala Sutta* (MN 90), which likewise examines the question of omniscience [DharmaNexus; Le 2018]. Cross-linguistic matches are automatically identified with Sanskrit texts such as the *Saṅghabhedavastu* and *Lalitavistara*, as well as Chinese Āgama discourses in the *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26) and *Dīrgha Āgama* (T 1) [DharmaNexus]. The sutta has been translated into English by I.B. Horner, Ñāṇamoli Thera, and Bhikkhu Sujato [SuttaCentral].
